questions.question: The Kruskal method builds a minimum spanning tree of a connected undirected network with edge lengths, starting with no selected edges. Which step does it repeat?
options: Select a shortest unselected edge that has at least one endpoint not yet touched.
At every vertex, select the shortest edge there, then remove edges that form cycles.
Select a shortest unselected edge that creates no cycle with the edges already selected.
Select a shortest edge joining the current tree to a new vertex, starting from one vertex.

questions.question: Midway through the Kruskal method on a connected undirected network with edge lengths, what can be said about the edges selected so far?
options: They always form one connected tree, as in every step.
They contain no cycle but may form several separate pieces.
They may contain a cycle, which is removed at the very end.
They always include an edge at the vertex chosen to start.

questions.question: When does the Kruskal method, run on a connected undirected network with edge lengths, stop selecting edges?
options: Only after every edge of the network has been inspected once
As soon as every vertex is an endpoint of some selected edge
As soon as the selected edges connect all vertices together
As soon as one edge has been rejected for creating a cycle

questions.question: In the Kruskal method, the shortest unselected edges are two edges of length 3, and neither creates a cycle. How does the method continue?
options: Either may be inspected first; the final total is unaffected.
The one whose endpoints have the lower labels comes first.
Both are rejected, since the choice between them is left unclear.
Neither is used until a unique shortest edge is found.

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 3, $A$–$C$ 1, $B$–$C$ 2, $B$–$D$ 5, $C$–$D$ 4, $C$–$E$ 6, $D$–$E$ 2, $D$–$F$ 7, $E$–$F$ 5 (lengths after the edge names). Which edge is the first to be rejected by the Kruskal method?
options: $B$–$D$, of length 5
$C$–$D$, of length 4
$D$–$E$, of length 2
$A$–$B$, of length 3

questions.question: During the Kruskal method on a network with vertices $A$ to $F$, the selected edges are $A$–$B$, $B$–$C$, $D$–$E$ and $E$–$F$. Which of the following edges must be rejected if it is inspected next?
The Kruskal method is run on a connected network with 7 vertices. How many edges does it accept in total?
options: 6, one less than the number of vertices
7, one for each vertex of the network
21, one for each pair of the vertices
5, two less than the number of vertices

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 3, $A$–$C$ 1, $B$–$C$ 2, $B$–$D$ 5, $C$–$D$ 4, $C$–$E$ 6, $D$–$E$ 2, $D$–$F$ 7, $E$–$F$ 5 (lengths after the edge names). Which pieces do the selected edges form, isolated vertices included, after the Kruskal method has accepted three edges?

A network has edges $A$–$B$ 3, $A$–$C$ 1, $B$–$C$ 2, $B$–$D$ 5, $C$–$D$ 4, $C$–$E$ 6, $D$–$E$ 2, $D$–$F$ 7, $E$–$F$ 5 (lengths after the edge names). A student runs the Kruskal method but rejects every edge whose two endpoints are both already touched by selected edges. What goes wrong at $C$–$D$, of length 4?
options: $C$–$D$ is correctly rejected, as it closes a cycle through $B$.
$C$–$D$ is wrongly rejected, though it joins two separate pieces.
Nothing goes wrong, as the two rules always agree.
$C$–$D$ is wrongly accepted, since it is longer than $D$–$E$.

questions.question: In the Kruskal method, an edge was rejected because it would have created a cycle. Why will this edge never become acceptable later in the run?
options: Later edges are all longer, so it would no longer be the shortest.
It can become acceptable once its pieces merge with another one.
Each edge may be inspected once, whatever happens in later steps.
Selected edges are never removed, so its endpoints stay connected.

questions.question: During the Kruskal method on a connected network with $n$ vertices, the selected edges form $p$ separate pieces, each piece a tree and isolated vertices counted as pieces. Why does the method stop exactly when $n-1$ edges are accepted?
options: There are $n-p+1$ selected edges, so $n-1$ edges means $p=2$.
There are $p-1$ selected edges, so $n-1$ edges means $p=n$ pieces.
There are $n-1$ edges as soon as the rejected edges number $p$.
There are $n-p$ selected edges, so $n-1$ edges means $p=1$ piece.

questions.question: A network has edges $P$–$Q$ 4, $P$–$R$ 3, $Q$–$R$ 2, $Q$–$S$ 6, $R$–$S$ 5, $R$–$T$ 7, $S$–$T$ 1 (lengths after the edge names). Which edges does the Kruskal method select?
options: $S$–$T$, $Q$–$R$, $P$–$R$ and $P$–$Q$, of total 10
$S$–$T$, $Q$–$R$, $P$–$R$ and $R$–$S$, of total 11
$S$–$T$, $Q$–$R$, $P$–$R$ and $Q$–$S$, of total 12
$S$–$T$, $Q$–$R$, $P$–$Q$ and $R$–$S$, with total length 12

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 3, $A$–$C$ 1, $B$–$C$ 2, $B$–$D$ 5, $C$–$D$ 4, $C$–$E$ 6, $D$–$E$ 2, $D$–$F$ 7, $E$–$F$ 5 (lengths after the edge names); edges of equal length are inspected in alphabetical order. Which edges does the Kruskal method never inspect before it stops?
options: None, as every edge is inspected exactly once
$C$–$E$ and $D$–$F$, the two longest edges
Only $D$–$F$, the longest edge
$B$–$D$ and $C$–$E$, the rejected edges

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 3, $A$–$C$ 1, $B$–$C$ 2, $B$–$D$ 5, $C$–$D$ 4, $C$–$E$ 6, $D$–$E$ 2, $D$–$F$ 7, $E$–$F$ 5 (lengths after the edge names). The length of $C$–$D$ is changed from 4 to 6, all else equal. What is the total length of the tree the Kruskal method now returns?
The Kruskal method accepts an edge $e$ joining two separate pieces of its current selection. Why is accepting $e$ safe for reaching a minimum total?
options: $e$ is shorter than every edge not yet selected, including rejected ones.
Every minimum spanning tree must contain all the edges shorter than $e$.
A minimum tree without $e$ has an edge between the pieces, no shorter, to swap.
$e$ is safe only when all lengths in the network are different.

questions.question: The Kruskal method is applied, by mistake, to a network consisting of two parts with no edge between them: $A$–$B$ 2, $B$–$C$ 3, $A$–$C$ 4 and $D$–$E$ 1. What happens?
options: It joins the parts with its last edge, as all edges are used.
Every edge is inspected, and the stopping rule is never met.
It stops after $D$–$E$, the shortest edge, as one part is done.
It accepts $A$–$C$ to make up the edge count of a tree.

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 1, $C$–$D$ 1, $A$–$C$ 2, $B$–$C$ 2, $D$–$E$ 3, $C$–$E$ 3, $E$–$F$ 4 (lengths after the edge names). How many different trees can the Kruskal method return, if equal-length edges are inspected in any order?
options: 2, since only one of the ties gives a real choice
8, from three independent choices between two edges each
6, from counting the orders of all the tied edges
4, from two independent choices between two edges each
